concept.technique_name: unrolled cylinder turn as right-triangle hypotenuse

examples.problem_statement: A thread is wound on a cylinder such that it makes exactly twenty-four complete turns around the cylinder. The two ends of thread touch the top and bottom of cylinder. If cylinder has a radius of 15 cm and its curved surface area is 2880 cm^2 then find the length of the string:

solution.description: Divide the given curved surface area by 15, the value the book divides by, to recover the height of the cylinder.
Split that height across the twenty-four complete turns, giving the vertical rise of one turn; this is the 8 the book carries into its next line.
Treat one unrolled turn as the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 and 15, and take the square root of the sum of their squares to get the length of a single turn.
Multiply the length of one complete turn by the twenty-four turns to obtain the total length of the thread.

key_reminders: Curved surface area of a cylinder divided by its circumference term gives the height.
Each unrolled turn of a helically wound thread is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the rise per turn and the horizontal run per turn.
Total thread length is the length of one turn times the number of turns.
common_mistakes: Reporting the height 192 cm or the single-turn length 17 cm as the final answer instead of multiplying by the 24 turns.
Using the full height 192 rather than the per-turn rise 8 as the vertical leg of the right triangle.

concept.technique_name: chaining two ratios through a common term using least common multiples

examples.problem_statement: At a certain fruit stand, there is a 2 to 5 ratio of pomelos to quinces and a 2 to 7 ratio of quinces to raspberries. Which of the following could be the number of pomelos at the stand? Select all that apply. (A) 2 (B) 4 (C) 6 (D) 8 (E) 10

solution.description: Multiply both values of the first ratio by 2, the multiplier the book prescribes, so that the quince term becomes the least common multiple 10.
Multiply both values of the second ratio by 5, the book's second multiplier, so its quince term also becomes 10.
Join the two scaled ratios on their now-common number of quinces to read off the single combined ratio, whose pomelo term is 4.
Conclude that the actual number of pomelos must be a multiple of 4, then keep only the answer choices that are multiples of 4.

key_reminders: To chain two ratios, scale each so the shared quantity takes the same value, using the least common multiple of its two terms.
Scaling a ratio means multiplying every term in it by the same factor.
In a combined ratio, an actual count must be a whole-number multiple of its ratio term.
common_mistakes: Reading the pomelo term as 2 from the unscaled first ratio and selecting 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 as all possible.
Selecting only 4 and forgetting that any multiple of 4, including 8, also qualifies.

examples.problem_statement: What is the percent increase from 50 to 60? %

solution.description: Subtract the original value from the new value to get the difference called for by the percent change formula.
Divide that difference by the original value 50, reducing the fraction to one fifth, which is 0.2.
Multiply the decimal by 100 to express the change as a percent.

key_reminders: Percent change equals the difference divided by the original value.
The original value is the one you start from, here 50, not the new value 60.
A decimal becomes a percent when multiplied by 100.
common_mistakes: Dividing the difference 10 by the new value 60 instead of the original 50, which gives about 16.7% rather than 20%.

concept.technique_name: congruent alternate angles across a transversal of parallel lines

examples.problem_statement: In the figure above, line k is parallel to line m. What is the value of y ? y =

solution.operation: (2y)^\circ \text{ and } 35^\circ \text{ lie between } k \parallel m \text{ on opposite sides of the transversal}
solution.description: Locate the two marked angles in the figure: both sit between the parallel lines k and m and on opposite sides of the line crossing them, so they are congruent.
Translate that congruence from the figure into an equation setting the two angle measures equal.
Divide both sides of the equation by 2 to isolate y.

key_reminders: Angles between two parallel lines and on opposite sides of a transversal are congruent.
Translate a figure into an algebraic equation before solving.
The variable y is half the angle expression (2y), so the angle measure is not the answer itself.
common_mistakes: Answering 35 by reporting the angle measure instead of dividing by 2 to get y.
Treating the two angles as supplementary and writing 2y = 145 instead of congruent.
